A large but strong upper level ridge of high pressure that had been prevalent since Mid-August persisted over the Southern Plains and Lower Mississippi Valley through the 20th,  with compressional warming beneath the ridge contributing to continued warming across Southern Arkansas, North Louisiana, and extreme Eastern Texas. Sinking air beneath the ridge and strong insolation again allowed for afternoon temperatures to climb into the upper 90s to near 100 degrees over these areas. When combined with the high humidity, heat indices ranged from 105-110 degrees across much of Southwest Arkansas, North Louisiana, and extreme Eastern Texas.

Strong heating developed over portions of North Louisiana during the afternoon of August 13th, ahead of a weak upper level disturbance that lingered across portions of extreme Northeast Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, and Southwest Arkansas. As this weak disturbance began to weaken on the 14th-15th, upper level ridging began to amplify east across the region into the Lower Mississippi Valley, resulting in afternoon temperatures climbing into the mid 90s to near 100 degrees each day through the morning of the 19th, before the heat wave intensified further. When combined with the humidity, heat indices ranged from 105-110 degrees.

A light southerly wind on the backside of surface high pressure over the Lower Mississippi Valley maintained ample low level moisture and limited the extent of mixing, resulting in heat indices ranging from 105-110 degrees across the aforementioned areas.

Damage is weak and narrow along this part of the path and is confined to minor tree damage. From there the tornado crossed Saint Clair Rd and continued northeast, eventually crossing Browns Creek Rd. At this location a metal outbuilding was completely destroyed and thrown roughly 100 yards downstream with the tornado. A table was thrown roughly 300 yards west northwest of where it was placed. Minor damage to a frame home also occurred at the end point of the Wilda Tornado.
